paragraphs.paragraph: Distress, Fear, and the Search for Refuge
paragraphs.title: Distress, Fear, and the Search for Refuge

easy.explanation: He asks God to give ear to his prayer and hear his supplication.
easy.q: To whom does the speaker address his prayer?

easy.explanation: He says, “the terrors of death are fallen upon me.”
easy.q: What has fallen upon the speaker?

easy.explanation: He wishes he had wings like a dove so that he could fly away and be at rest.
easy.q: What does the speaker wish he had?

answers: To escape the storm and find refuge
medium.explanation: He wants to hasten his escape from the windy storm and tempest.
medium.q: Why does the speaker want to go far away?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes being overcome by intense fear.
medium.q: What does “horror hath overwhelmed me” mean?

answers: Prayer, fear, and the desire to flee
medium.explanation: He begins with prayer, describes terror, and then longs to escape into the wilderness.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the speaker’s condition?

answers: A desire to return to the city
challenge.explanation: The dove expresses the speaker’s wish to fly away from distress and find rest.
challenge.q: What does the dove’s wings symbolize in this passage?

challenge.explanation: The windy storm and tempest reflect the speaker’s inner turmoil and fear.
challenge.q: How does the storm relate to the speaker’s inner condition?

answers: The speaker is indifferent to his situation
He is certain he needs no help
He is in distress and urgently seeks an answer
challenge.explanation: His repeated appeals for God to hear him show the urgency of his supplication.
challenge.q: What does the repeated request for God to hear emphasize?

paragraphs.idea: Distress, Fear, and the Search for Refuge

paragraphs.paragraph: A City Filled with Violence and Deceit
paragraphs.title: A City Filled with Violence and Deceit

easy.explanation: He says, “Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask the Lord to do to the enemies’ tongues?

easy.explanation: The speaker has seen violence and strife in the city.
easy.q: What is found in the city?

easy.explanation: The enemies go about the city’s walls day and night.
easy.q: When do trouble and wickedness surround the city?

medium.explanation: The speaker asks God to disrupt the enemies’ united and harmful speech.
medium.q: What does “divide their tongues” mean in context?

medium.explanation: The city is marked by violence, strife, wickedness, and deceit.

answers: It shows trouble both around the city and within it
It shows a city completely protected
medium.explanation: Trouble is present around the walls, in the midst of the city, and in its streets.
medium.q: How does the description of the walls and streets strengthen the picture of the city?

answers: Its walls cannot protect it from corruption within
challenge.explanation: Although the city has walls, violence and deceit permeate its inner life.
challenge.q: What is the significance of a walled city that is filled with violence?

answers: Deceit exists only outside the city
Deceit is part of the city’s public life
People in the city have no relationships
challenge.explanation: The streets, where communal life occurs, are continually marked by deceit.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the words “deceit and guile depart not from her streets”?

answers: The danger involves the enemies’ speech and schemes
The speaker wants to learn languages
challenge.explanation: The enemies’ speech is connected with the violence, strife, and schemes in the city.
challenge.q: Why is the request to divide the tongues appropriate to the city’s condition?

paragraphs.idea: A City Filled with Violence and Deceit

easy.explanation: The speaker says that if it had been an enemy, he could have borne it.
easy.q: Who was not the person reproaching the speaker?

answers: He was the speaker’s equal, guide, and acquaintance
He was only the speaker’s king
easy.explanation: The man is called “a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.”
easy.q: What was the relationship between the speaker and the man who hurt him?

answers: That death seize them and they go down into hell
easy.explanation: He asks that death seize them and that they go down into hell.
easy.q: What does the speaker ask concerning the wicked?

answers: The companion shared close counsel and worship with him
The enemy was weaker than he was
The companion lived in the wilderness
medium.explanation: The companion shared sweet counsel with him and walked with him to the house of God.
medium.q: Why does the companion’s betrayal hurt more than an enemy’s attack?

answers: They shared intimate counsel and conversation
medium.explanation: The phrase describes close fellowship and shared counsel.
medium.q: What does “we took sweet counsel together” mean?

answers: Closeness and trust versus persecution and betrayal
The wilderness versus the city only
medium.explanation: A trusted companion has become a persecutor, making the betrayal especially painful.
medium.q: What central contrast appears in this passage?

answers: The companion was never close to him
challenge.explanation: They worshiped together, so the betrayal violates both personal and spiritual trust.
challenge.q: What does the mention of walking to the house of God emphasize?

answers: An enemy’s attack would have been more expected
The speaker did not know his enemies
The speaker did not suffer betrayal
challenge.explanation: The speaker says that an enemy’s attack would have been easier to bear.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from “it was not an enemy that reproached me”?

answers: He asks God to judge people marked by violence and wickedness
He asks God to reward them
He asks to escape from them into the wilderness
challenge.explanation: He describes wickedness among them and asks that judgment come upon them.
challenge.q: How does the requested judgment relate to the description of the wicked?

easy.explanation: He says, “I will call upon God; and the LORD shall save me.”
easy.q: To whom does the speaker call for salvation?

easy.explanation: He prays and cries aloud in the evening, morning, and at noon.
easy.q: At what times does the speaker pray?

easy.explanation: God delivered his soul in peace from the battle that was against him.
easy.q: From what was the speaker delivered?

answers: Prayer strengthens his confidence that the Lord will hear him
Prayer causes him to stop asking
Prayer shows that he does not believe in God
medium.explanation: He prays at different times while trusting that the Lord will hear his voice.
medium.q: What is the connection between continual prayer and the speaker’s confidence?

medium.explanation: “Delivered” means rescued or brought safely out of danger.
medium.q: What does “delivered” mean in “He hath delivered my soul”?

medium.explanation: He says, “for there were many with me.”
medium.q: Who was with the speaker during the battle?

answers: His appeal to God is continual
He prays only during one danger
challenge.explanation: The three times of day emphasize persistence in prayer.
challenge.q: What does the sequence “evening, and morning, and at noon” emphasize?

answers: Trust in God’s hearing leads to hope and rescue
It removes the need for prayer
It replaces God with human support
challenge.explanation: The speaker trusts that God will hear and recalls being delivered from battle.
challenge.q: How does confidence that God will hear relate to the description of deliverance?

answers: Deliverance is described with divine help and the presence of supporters
Deliverance comes only through the enemy
The many are described as indifferent
challenge.explanation: The passage mentions both God’s action and the many who were with the speaker.
challenge.q: What is the significance of combining God’s help with the support of many?

paragraphs.paragraph: Hypocrisy, Deceit, and Trust in God
paragraphs.title: Hypocrisy, Deceit, and Trust in God

answers: He carried it to the city
easy.explanation: The text says, “he hath broken his covenant.”
easy.q: What did the enemy do to his covenant?

easy.explanation: His words are smooth, but “war was in his heart.”
easy.q: What lies behind the enemy’s smooth words?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Cast thy burden upon the LORD.”
easy.q: Upon whom is the speaker told to cast his burden?

answers: His words are songs of joy
medium.explanation: The smooth words are deceptive because war and drawn swords lie behind them.
medium.q: What is meant by the enemy’s words being “smoother than butter”?

answers: He will sustain him and not let the righteous be moved
He will hide him in the wilderness
medium.explanation: The Lord promises to sustain him and never suffer the righteous to be moved.
medium.q: What does the Lord promise to the one who casts his burden upon Him?

answers: Smooth words and deceit versus trust and confidence in God
The city versus the wilderness only
medium.explanation: The enemy hides hostility behind smooth speech, while the speaker trusts in the Lord.
medium.q: What is the central contrast in these verses?

answers: A pleasant outward appearance does not prove good intentions
The enemy does not intend to harm anyone
challenge.explanation: The passage warns that agreeable speech may conceal hostile intentions.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the contrast between smooth words and war in the heart?

answers: It places trust in God over against the fate of deceitful men
It strengthens the power of deceivers
It removes the idea of judgment
challenge.explanation: Trust in the Lord contrasts with the judgment promised to bloody and deceitful men.
challenge.q: How does the command to cast one’s burden upon the Lord connect with the end of the passage?

answers: The Lord will sustain and preserve the righteous
The righteous have no need of faith
challenge.explanation: The statement expresses confidence that God will uphold the righteous.
challenge.q: What does “he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” mean here?

paragraphs.idea: Hypocrisy, Deceit, and Trust in God
